glosses: trouble, unpleasantness (unpleasant behaviour, occurrence, etc.)
nieprzyjemna sytuacja albo rzecz
The property of being unpleasant or disagreeable.

examples.text: Given the behaviour of the members, who do normally come to Lord’s, this seemed a bizarre attempt to offload the unpleasantness on hoi polloi taking advantage of some rare £25 tickets.

glosses: An unpleasant behaviour, occurrence, etc.

examples.text: Perhaps you are not so much aware as I am, of the mischief that may, of the unpleasantnesses that must, arise from a young man’s being received in this manner—domesticated among us—authorized to come at all hours—and placed suddenly on a footing which must do away all restraints.

glosses: A distressing or dangerous situation.

examples.text: He was in trouble when the rain started.

glosses: A difficulty, problem, condition, or action contributing to such a situation.

examples.text: The trouble was a leaking brake line.
The bridge column magnified the trouble with a slight tilt in the wrong direction.
Lest the fiend […] some new trouble raise.
Foul whisperings are abroad; unnatural deeds / Do breed unnatural troubles.

glosses: A person liable to place others or themselves in such a situation.

examples.text:
’Cause I knew you were trouble when you walked in
So shame on me no-ow

glosses: The state of being troubled, disturbed, or distressed mentally; unease, disquiet.

examples.text:
Yet oft when sundown skirts the moor
⁠An inner trouble I behold,
⁠A spectral doubt which makes me cold,
That I shall be thy mate no more, […]

glosses: Objectionable feature of something or someone; problem, drawback, weakness, failing, or shortcoming.

examples.text: Your trouble is that you quit too readily.
The trouble with that suggestion is that we lack the funds to put it in motion.

glosses: Violent or turbulent occurrence or event; unrest, disturbance.

examples.text: the troubles in Northern Ireland

“I don’t know how you and the ‘head,’ as you call him, will get on, but I do know that if you call my duds a ‘livery’ again there’ll be trouble. It’s bad enough to go around togged out like a life saver on a drill day, but I can stand that ’cause I'm paid for it. What I won’t stand is to have them togs called a livery. […]”

glosses: Efforts taken or expended, typically beyond the normal required.

examples.text: It’s no trouble for me to edit it.
She never took the trouble to close them.
Indeed, by the report of our elders, this nervous preparation for old age is only trouble thrown away.

glosses: Difficulty in doing something.

examples.text: She has trouble eating.

glosses: Health problems, ailment, generally of some particular part of the body.

examples.text: He’s been in hospital with some heart trouble.

glosses: A malfunction.

examples.text: My old car has engine trouble.

glosses: Liability to punishment; conflict with authority.

examples.text: He had some trouble with the law.

glosses: A fault or interruption in a stratum.
Wife. Clipping of trouble and strife.
An unplanned, unwanted or undesired pregnancy.

examples.text: I never had schoolin’ but he taught me well / With his smooth southern style / Three months later I’m a gal in trouble / And I haven’t seen him for a while.

glosses: To disturb, stir up, agitate (a medium, especially water).

examples.text: For an Angel went downe at a certaine season into the poole, and troubled the water:
God looking forth will trouble all his Hoſt

glosses: To mentally distress; to cause (someone) to be anxious or perplexed.

examples.text: What she said about narcissism is troubling me.
Now is my soule troubled, and what shall I say? Father, saue me from this houre, but for this cause came I vnto this houre.
Take the Boy to you: he ſo troubles me, / ’Tis paſt enduring.
Never trouble your ſelf about thoſe Faults in them, which you know Age will cure.

glosses: In weaker sense: to bother or inconvenience.

examples.text: I will not trouble you to deliver the letter.

glosses: To physically afflict.

examples.text: My bad knee is troubling me.

glosses: To take pains (to do something); to bother.

examples.text: I won’t trouble to post the letter today; I can do it tomorrow.
« The hut’s not very tidy, if you don’t mind, » he said. « I cleared it what I could. » / « But I didn’t want you to trouble! » she said.

glosses: To worry; to be anxious.

examples.text: Why trouble about the future? It is wholly uncertain.

glosses: Chose désagréable, sujet de chagrin, d’ennui, de dégoût.

examples.text: C’est un grand désagrément que d’avoir des procès.
Il a eu, il a essuyé de grands désagréments dans l’exercice de son emploi.
Il s’est attiré des désagréments.
On n’en a que du désagrément.

Faillible, humain donc, ses faiblesses qui l’amènent à son funeste destin permettent l’identification, la projection des sentiments du spectateur, pouvant susciter un pathos si la cohérence de l’œuvre est suffisante, les péripéties et infortunes diverses produisant un désagrément au fond tellement bienvenu !

glosses: Événement fâcheux.

examples.text: Il conta sa mésaventure au mayeur qui, feignant d’y compatir, lui permit de choisir, à moitié prix, dans le troupeau, une bête toute parelle.
Mais tout est bien qui finit bien, et il ne me reste plus qu'à aller conter ma mésaventure au commissaire de police en lui remettant ce carnet en cuir de Russie […]

Un certain type de découvertes se présente avec une curieuse insistance dans les sciences biologiques : ces catastrophes de laboratoires qui ouvrent soudain la voie du salut, ces expériences gâchées grâce auxquelles, non sans perversité, se révèle la solution, parce que l'attention de l'expérimentateur a été brutalement attiré sur l'aspect inverse du problème. C'est ce que l'on pourrait appeler « découverte par mésaventure ».

Autre leçon de cet échec balzacien : il ne suffit pas d'être célèbre pour avoir fût-ce un succès d'estime, au théâtre. Les mésaventures de personnalités tout-parisiennes l'ont prouvé encore récemment. C'est finalement assez moral, […].

Si Hostrup faisait marche arrière aujourd'hui, toutes les mésaventures qu'il avait subies pour faire plier Mørk n'auraient plus aucun sens et rimeraient tout au plus avec fiasco. Hostrup ne pouvait plus faire marche arrière.

glosses: Sensación de rechazo o repulsión; reacción o sentimiento frente a algo o alguien que no es grato o que se considera desagradable.
Expresión en la comunicación o en el rostro que indica desagrado₁, contrariedad o disgusto.
Primera persona del singular (yo) del presente de indicativo de desagradar.
Se dice de la persona o animal doméstico muy tozudo o pesado y que incordia en exceso.

examples.text: ¡Qué tío más pejiguera!

glosses: Contrariedad
Enojo, enfado, ira, molestia.
Desagrado, sensación de molestia ante cosas desagradables o repulsivas

examples.text: „Ist der Schnelltest positiv, hat der Fahrer noch keine rechtlichen Folgen, wohl aber Unannehmlichkeiten zu befürchten.“

Ich würde gerne heute Nachmittag vorbeischauen, wenn es Ihnen keine Unannehmlichkeiten bereitet.

glosses: Unannehmlichkeit oder Ärger

examples.text: „Die Witze spiegeln sicher auch unsere Gemütslagen, Zeitstimmungen und persönliches Ungemach und Gemach wider.“
